items.title: Applying the Ratio Test for Convergence

sections.normalized_html: Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{3^n}] is convergent.
sections.readable_text: Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{3^n}] is convergent.

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{3^n}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get [MATH: \eqalign{ a_{n+1}= \frac{n+1}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n}. }]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{ L &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \div \frac{n}{3^n}\right)\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \frac{3^n}{n}\right)\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3n} \right)\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{n+1}{n}\right)\[5pt] &= \frac{1}{3}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)\[5pt] &=\frac{1}{3}\left(1 + 0\right)\[5pt] &=\frac{1}{3}. }]

Note that we dropped the absolute value bars because the sequence is positive for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]

Since [MATH: L = \dfrac{1}{3}<1,] we conclude that the series is convergent by the ratio test.
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{3^n}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get

a_{n+1}= \frac{n+1}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n}.
}]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
L
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\[5pt]
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \div \frac{n}{3^n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \frac{3^n}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3n} \right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{n+1}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \frac{1}{3}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&=\frac{1}{3}\left(1 + 0\right)\[5pt]
&=\frac{1}{3}.
}]

Note that we dropped the absolute value bars because the sequence is positive for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]

Since [MATH: L = \dfrac{1}{3}<1,] we conclude that the series is convergent by the ratio test.

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{3^n}] is convergent.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{3^n}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
a_{n+1}= \frac{n+1}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n}.
}]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
L
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\[5pt]
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \div \frac{n}{3^n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \frac{3^n}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3n} \right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{n+1}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \frac{1}{3}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&=\frac{1}{3}\left(1 + 0\right)\[5pt]
&=\frac{1}{3}.
}]

Note that we dropped the absolute value bars because the sequence is positive for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]

Since [MATH: L = \dfrac{1}{3}<1,] we conclude that the series is convergent by the ratio test.

items.title: Applying the Ratio Test for Divergence

sections.normalized_html: Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n\, n!}{3^n}] is divergent.
sections.readable_text: Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n\, n!}{3^n}] is divergent.

sections.normalized_html:
This is an example of an alternating series. The [MATH: (-1)^n] causes the signs of the successive terms to alternate between positive and negative.

Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{(-1)^n\,n!}{3^n}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get

[MATH: \eqalign{ a_{n+1}= \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}(n+1)!}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n}. }]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \require{cancel} L &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n} \div \dfrac{(-1)^n\,n!}{3^n}\right|\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \dfrac{3^n}{(-1)^n\,n!}\right|\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|-\dfrac{n+1}{3}\right|\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1 3\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(n+1\right)\[5pt] &=\infty. }]

Since [MATH: L=\infty > 1,] we conclude that the series is divergent by the ratio test.

items.title: Applying the Ratio Test in the Indeterminate Case

sections.normalized_html: Use the ratio test to determine whether the series [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}] is convergent or divergent.
sections.readable_text: Use the ratio test to determine whether the series [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}] is convergent or divergent.

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{2n+1}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get

[MATH: a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2(n+1)+1}= \frac{1}{2n+3}.]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(1)/(2n + 3) ÷ (1)/(2n + 1)|; = lim_(n → ∞)((1)/(2n + 3) ⋅ (2n + 1)/(1)); = lim_(n → ∞)((2n + 1)/(2n + 3)); = lim_(n → ∞)((2 + (1)/(n))/(2 + (3)/(n))); = (2)/(2); = 1.]

Since [MATH: L=1,] the ratio test gives no conclusion about whether the series is convergent or divergent.

Note: Although the ratio test gave no conclusion, the series [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}] is actually divergent.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The ratio test can allow us to determine whether an infinite series converges or diverges, based on the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of consecutive terms.

Content:
Let the number [MATH: L\geq 0] be defined as
[MATH: L = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|.]
The ratio test states that:

Content:
- if [MATH: L<1,] then the series is convergent
- if [MATH: L>1,] then the series is divergent
- if [MATH: L=1,] then the ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence or divergence of the series

Content:
Note: There is some nice intuition behind the ratio test. Loosely speaking, we can think of the series as eventually looking similar to a geometric series whose common ratio has magnitude [MATH: L.]

Content:
- If [MATH: L<1,] then the terms of the series decrease in magnitude, so it's intuitive that they would converge (rather than diverge).
- If [MATH: L>1,] then the terms of the series increase in magnitude, so it's intuitive that they would diverge.

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying the Ratio Test for Convergence

Example Prompt:
Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{3^n}] is convergent.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{n}{3^n}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get
[MATH: \eqalign{
a_{n+1}= \frac{n+1}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n}.
}]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
L
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\[5pt]
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \div \frac{n}{3^n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \frac{3^n}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3n} \right)\[5pt]
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{n+1}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&= \frac{1}{3}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)\[5pt]
&=\frac{1}{3}\left(1 + 0\right)\[5pt]
&=\frac{1}{3}.
}]

Note that we dropped the absolute value bars because the sequence is positive for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]

Since [MATH: L = \dfrac{1}{3}<1,] we conclude that the series is convergent by the ratio test.

---

Item 5 — Example: Applying the Ratio Test for Divergence

Example Prompt:
Use the ratio test to show that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n\, n!}{3^n}] is divergent.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
This is an example of an alternating series. The [MATH: (-1)^n] causes the signs of the successive terms to alternate between positive and negative.

Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{(-1)^n\,n!}{3^n}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get

[MATH: \eqalign{
a_{n+1}= \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}(n+1)!}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n}.
}]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\require{cancel}
L
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\[5pt]
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n} \div \dfrac{(-1)^n\,n!}{3^n}\right|\[5pt]
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \dfrac{3^n}{(-1)^n\,n!}\right|\[5pt]
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|-\dfrac{n+1}{3}\right|\[5pt]
&=\dfrac 1 3\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(n+1\right)\[5pt]
&=\infty.
}]

Since [MATH: L=\infty > 1,] we conclude that the series is divergent by the ratio test.

Item 8 — Example: Applying the Ratio Test in the Indeterminate Case

Example Prompt:
Use the ratio test to determine whether the series [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}] is convergent or divergent.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: a_n = \dfrac{1}{2n+1}.] If we replace [MATH: n] with [MATH: n+1,] we get

[MATH: a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2(n+1)+1}= \frac{1}{2n+3}.]

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: a_{n+1},] we can work out the necessary limit:

[MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|(1)/(2n + 3) ÷ (1)/(2n + 1)|; = lim_(n → ∞)((1)/(2n + 3) ⋅ (2n + 1)/(1)); = lim_(n → ∞)((2n + 1)/(2n + 3)); = lim_(n → ∞)((2 + (1)/(n))/(2 + (3)/(n))); = (2)/(2); = 1.]

Since [MATH: L=1,] the ratio test gives no conclusion about whether the series is convergent or divergent.

Note: Although the ratio test gave no conclusion, the series [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}] is actually divergent.
